title: Ledger A: the Bookkeeper, the Combination, and the Dime
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Richford, the farm on Michigan Hill
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Rockefeller Archive Center, 'John D. Rockefeller, 1839-1937'). The coordinate is an estimate read off the description 'three miles east of Richford'; the farmhouse site lies inside Michigan Hill State Forest and no surveyed marker point was found.
stops.campa: A hilltop farm three miles east of Richford, in the hard country south of the Finger Lakes. The second of six children is born to William Avery Rockefeller and Eliza Davison Rockefeller on the eighth of July. The father deals in patent remedies and is away for months together; the mother keeps the house, the children, and the Baptist discipline the boy will not put down for ninety-seven years. The farmhouse is gone and the fields have grown back into state forest.
suggested_refs: The Michigan Hill farm site near Richford, Tioga County, New York
sources: PBS American Experience, 'John D. Rockefeller, Senior'

stops.name: Moravia, the boyhood house in Cayuga County
stops.date_confidence: the Moravia years run roughly 1843-1850 with no attested single date; the earliest year is used to order the segment. Coordinate converted from the Historical Marker Database marker, 42 deg 45.909' N, 76 deg 27.321' W.
stops.campa: The family moves again, to the Moravia country of Cayuga County, one of a string of upstate removals driven by the father's traveling trade. William Avery is on the road selling; the household is what Eliza makes of it, and every sum in it is counted twice. The boy raises turkeys and sells them, lends fifty dollars to a neighboring farmer at seven percent, and enters both transactions in a book. A historical marker stands today where the house stood.
suggested_refs: The 'John D. Rockefeller Boyhood Home' marker, Cayuga County, New York
sources: Historical Marker Database (hmdb.org), 'John D. Rockefeller Boyhood Home'

stops.name: Owego, the academy on the Susquehanna
stops.date_confidence: PBS materials disagree on the year the family reached Owego, 1849 or 1851; the conflict was not resolved by anything reachable and the later year is used only to order the segment. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He is sent to Owego Academy, a schooling somewhat above the family's means, in a river town on the Susquehanna where his father's absences are lengthening and the mother's economies are tightening around them. He is not quick in class and he is not slow. He is exact. Arithmetic he does well, and singing, which he keeps up all his life, and he already keeps his own accounts in a hand that will not change in eighty years. Then in 1853 the family crosses into Ohio, and the academy is behind him with everything else in that country.
suggested_refs: Owego Academy, Tioga County, New York
sources: PBS American Experience, 'John D. Rockefeller, Senior' biography and timeline

stops.name: Strongsville, the family reaches Ohio
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Rockefeller Archive Center); month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The Rockefellers reach Ohio and settle first at Strongsville, southwest of Cleveland, among relations who take them in. William Avery installs the family and departs again on his rounds, as he has done in every town so far. The boy is fourteen. A few miles northeast lies Cleveland: a lake port at the mouth of a canal, three trunk lines converging on it, a crooked river bending through flats where anything at all can be landed, stored, refined, and shipped on again.
suggested_refs: Strongsville, Cuyahoga County, first Ohio settlement of the Rockefeller family

stops.name: Cleveland, Central High on Prospect Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attendance attested 1853-1855; month set to order the segment. Coordinate corrected: the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History places Central High in the 1850s in the basement of a Universalist church on Prospect Avenue, roughly 400m from the Public Square point given in the research pool, which that pool reused for four separate scenes. Note also that the same Encyclopedia article does not mention Rockefeller as a pupil at all; it names his wife as a graduate.
stops.campa: He enters Central High in Cleveland, which in these years holds its classes in the basement of a Universalist church on Prospect Avenue, the city having not yet built it a house of its own. He studies there about two years and leaves in 1855 without the diploma, by one account two months short of it. What he wants is not the certificate. He wants a stool in a counting house, and no certificate in Ohio gets him one. Laura Spelman is in these rooms with him. She takes her diploma, and years afterward gives the school its clock tower.
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, 'Central High School'
sources: PBS American Experience, 'John D. Rockefeller, Senior'
Case Western Reserve University, Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, 'Central High School'

stops.name: Cleveland, baptized at Erie Street Baptist
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day default to 01. Coordinate corrected to Eagle Street at Erie (E. 9th), where the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History says the congregation first met, about 800m from the point in the research pool. The often-repeated detail that he was church clerk by 1858 and trustee by 1860 is Chernow's, not that Encyclopedia's, which records only a trustee term in 1883; the discrepancy is left standing.
stops.campa: He is baptized into the Erie Street Baptist Church, a poor congregation meeting near Eagle Street on the east side, and it becomes the fixed point of his life outside business. He joins as a teenager, gives to it out of his first wages, in recorded amounts, and rises in its offices; Chernow has him church clerk at nineteen, while the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History records only a trustee's term in 1883. The doctrine he takes from it is not complicated: money is a thing entrusted, the getting of it is a duty and the giving of it is a duty, and somebody keeps the account.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Rockefeller; quoted verbatim in Ron Chernow, Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr. (1998), ch. 3, whose endnote cites John T. Flynn, God's Gold (1932), p. 395
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, 'Euclid Ave. Baptist Church', successor to the Erie Street congregation
sources: Case Western Reserve University, Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, 'Euclid Ave. Baptist Church'

stops.name: Cleveland, Folsom's Mercantile College
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Rockefeller Archive Center); month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He enrolls at Folsom's Mercantile College for a course advertised at six months: bookkeeping, penmanship, commercial paper, the forms of exchange. He finishes it in about three and takes the certificate. The habit is older than the school and the school only formalizes it. Forty years on, the men working under him at Standard Oil will find that every barrel, every hoop, every drop of solder on a five-gallon can is being counted somewhere by somebody who answers to him.
stops.quote: From early boyhood I kept a little book which I remember I called Ledger A -- and this little volume is still preserved.
stops.quote_source: John D. Rockefeller, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Chapter II, 'The Difficult Art of Getting'
suggested_refs: Ledger A, Rockefeller's boyhood account book, preserved at the Rockefeller Archive Center
sources: Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Project Gutenberg #17090

stops.name: Cleveland, Hewitt and Tuttle and the first Job Day
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Rockefeller Archive Center). Exact office address unconfirmed; the coordinate is placed in the Flats and riverfront commission-house district where such firms stood.
stops.campa: After six weeks of walking the commission houses along the river asking for work, he is taken on as assistant bookkeeper by Hewitt and Tuttle, produce shippers on the Cleveland docks. Wages are settled afterward and come to about fifty cents a day. He keeps the anniversary of this morning every year for the rest of his life, calls it Job Day, and marks it more warmly than his birthday. Ida Tarbell, who would spend three years taking his enterprise apart in print, described the clerk he was.
stops.quote: one of the early-and-late sort, who saw everything, forgot nothing and never talked
stops.quote_source: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), Chapter II
suggested_refs: The Hewitt and Tuttle commission house, Cleveland riverfront
sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), Project Gutenberg #60692

stops.name: Cleveland, Clark and Rockefeller open their books
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Rockefeller Archive Center); month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: At nineteen he leaves other men's books to keep his own. With a thousand dollars saved and a thousand borrowed from his father at ten percent, he goes into partnership with Maurice B. Clark as commission merchants in grain, hay, meats, and whatever else moves through the port. The war comes two years later and the armies need every article they broker. The firm clears more in its war years than either partner had counted on in a decade of ordinary trade.
stops.quote: a genius for seeing the possibilities in material things
stops.quote_source: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), Chapter II
suggested_refs: The Clark and Rockefeller commission office, Cleveland
sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

stops.name: Kingsbury Run, the refinery and the substitute
stops.date_confidence: the refinery partnership is attested to 1863 (Rockefeller Archive Center); month and day default to 01. The substitute is tagged [R]: National Archives research on an 1863 Cleveland enrollment record, entered under the probable clerical error 'John W. Rockefeller', is reported in biographical treatments as strong evidence that he paid for one, as the Enrollment Act allowed. The original document was not viewed. Refinery site placed in the Cuyahoga and Kingsbury Run refining corridor; the exact plat is unverified.
stops.campa: Oil has been coming out of the Pennsylvania ground for four years and arriving in Cleveland by the barrel and the tank car. He looks at the drilling and sees a lottery. He looks at refining and sees a manufacture, which can be measured. With Clark and an English mechanic named Samuel Andrews he puts up works on the flats at Kingsbury Run. The same year his name goes onto a Cleveland enrollment list and he does not go to the war; he pays for a substitute, which the law allows, and stays with the stills.
stops.quote: He had the frugal man's hatred of waste and disorder, of middlemen and unnecessary manipulation.
stops.quote_source: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), Chapter II
suggested_refs: The Andrews, Clark & Co. works at Kingsbury Run, Cleveland
sources: National Archives research on Civil War enrollment records, as summarized in biographical treatments
Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

stops.name: Cleveland, the marriage to Laura Spelman
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Rockefeller Archive Center). The venue is not settled by the sources reached, which allow either a church or the Spelman residence; the coordinate is a general downtown Cleveland point and should not be read as a building.
stops.campa: He marries Laura Celestia Spelman on the eighth of September. They had known each other in the city's school circles since Central High, where she took the diploma he did not. She is serious in the same Baptist way he is serious, and she is the one person outside the business whose judgment he will take without arguing it. He is twenty-five, with a refinery and a commission house behind him and nothing yet that anybody outside Cleveland has heard of.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Archive Center, 'Laura Spelman Rockefeller'

stops.name: Niagara Falls, the honeymoon
stops.date_confidence: the honeymoon is attested to 1864 (Rockefeller Archive Center, 'Laura Spelman Rockefeller'); the day is set only to place it after the eighth of September wedding. Coordinate is the American Falls; a second coordinate in the research pool, 43.0962 / -79.0377, lies about four kilometres inland and is discarded.
stops.campa: The wedding journey runs north to Niagara, where he looks at the falls, then into Canada and on through New England before turning back to Cleveland. It is the longest journey he has made and near the longest he will ever make. The record of his movements, over ninety-seven years, is a short domestic circuit: two counties of upstate New York, Cleveland, the lower end of Manhattan, a ridge above the Hudson at Pocantico, a pine town in the New Jersey barrens, and a beach in Florida.
suggested_refs: The American Falls at Niagara

stops.name: Kingsbury Run, the auction and the man from the Erie
stops.date_confidence: the auction is attested to 1865 and Flagler's entry to 1867 (Rockefeller Archive Center); month and day default to 01, and the two events are carried in one stop at the same works.
stops.campa: The partnership breaks over the oil. Clark wants caution; Rockefeller wants to borrow and build. They agree to auction the refinery between themselves, and the bidding climbs past every figure either man had in his head until Clark stops at seventy-two thousand five hundred dollars and Rockefeller does not. He is twenty-five and owns the largest refinery in Cleveland. Two years later a grain and salt man named Henry Morrison Flagler comes in with Stephen Harkness's capital behind him and takes the desk facing his.
stops.quote: It was a friendship founded on business, which Mr. Flagler used to say was a good deal better than a business founded on friendship.
stops.quote_source: John D. Rockefeller, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Chapter I, 'Some Old Friends'
suggested_refs: The firm of Rockefeller, Andrews & Flagler, Cleveland, 1867
sources: Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Project Gutenberg #17090

stops.name: Cleveland, the Standard Oil Company is chartered
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Rockefeller Archive Center). Exact office address not confirmed; the coordinate is the same general downtown Cleveland point used for the 1864 marriage, and marks the business district rather than a building.
stops.campa: On the tenth of January the Standard Oil Company is incorporated under the laws of Ohio with a million dollars of capital: Rockefeller, his brother William, Andrews, Flagler, Harkness, and a few others. PBS reckons his own share at about thirty percent. The name is a promise to the buyer, a kerosene of uniform quality that will not explode in a lamp, in a trade where refiners' quality varies enough to kill people. On the day it is chartered the company controls perhaps a tenth of American refining.
suggested_refs: The Ohio articles of incorporation of the Standard Oil Company, 10 January 1870
sources: PBS American Experience, 'John D. Rockefeller, Senior'

stops.name: Titusville, the Oil Region rises against the South Improvement Company
stops.date_confidence: the episode is attested to 1872 (Tarbell, reproducing the charter and the railroad contracts); the month is set only to order the segment. Rockefeller's own presence in the oil region during the 1872 uproar is not documented in anything reached; this stop records the geography of the revolt, not a visit.
stops.campa: The trunk railroads sign contracts with the South Improvement Company, a shell in which Standard men hold stock: fixed freight rates, rebates on their own shipments, and drawbacks paid to them out of what their competitors pay to ship. The producers learn the schedule and rise. Titusville, Oil City, and Petroleum Centre shut the wells, refuse to sell to the combination, and carry the papers to Harrisburg and Washington. The scheme collapses before it ever operates. His own account of those years, written thirty-seven years later, is flat.
stops.quote: We did not ruthlessly go after the trade of our competitors and attempt to ruin it by cutting prices or instituting a spy system.
stops.quote_source: John D. Rockefeller, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Chapter III, 'The Standard Oil Company'
suggested_refs: The South Improvement Company charter and railroad contracts, reproduced in Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)
sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

stops.name: Cleveland, the refiners sold in three months
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1872 (Rockefeller Archive Center; Tarbell); the month is set to place the acquisitions after the South Improvement disclosure. Whether particular sales were voluntary or coerced remains a live dispute and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: While the oil region is in the streets, Standard's men work the Cleveland refiners one at a time, quietly, with the books open. Take stock in the Standard, they say, or take cash, but sell. In a few months nearly every competing firm in the city is gone. Some who took stock died rich. Some who took cash spent the rest of their lives saying they had been robbed. Isaac Hewitt, the man who gave him his first job seventeen years earlier, was among the sellers, and testified afterward to what Rockefeller said when he asked why the price should be believed.
stops.quote: I have ways of making money that you know nothing of.
stops.quote_source: Rockefeller to Isaac Hewitt, as Hewitt testified in 1879, reported verbatim in Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), Chapter II
suggested_refs: Hewitt's 1879 testimony on the Cleveland sales, in Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company
sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904), Project Gutenberg #60692

stops.name: The Allegheny pipeline country, Tidewater against National Transit
stops.date_confidence: the Tidewater struggle runs 1878-1883 and the Empire Transportation fight belongs to 1877 (Rockefeller Archive Center); the earliest year orders the segment, month and day default to 01. The coordinate marks the general Pennsylvania pipeline corridor and not a single site; this is an infrastructural stop, not a personal visit.
stops.campa: The producers try to get out from under the railroads by building their own line, a six-inch pipe carried over the Alleghenies against grades nobody has pumped oil across before. It works. Standard answers by laying pipe faster and further, buying rights of way ahead of its rivals, and folding the whole system into National Transit; within a few years it holds a controlling interest in Tidewater itself. The year before, the Pennsylvania Railroad had fought the same fight through the Empire Transportation Company and ended by selling Standard its refineries and its pipe.
suggested_refs: The Tidewater Pipe Company line and the National Transit system, north-central Pennsylvania

stops.name: Clarion, the indictment for conspiracy
stops.date_confidence: indictment attested to the day, and the nolle prosequi to 5 February 1880 (Tarbell, reproducing the legal material). The research pool's note that Pennsylvania's governor refused extradition is corrected here: Tarbell shows a Pennsylvania requisition lying undecided with the governor of NEW YORK, where Rockefeller then lived, and withdrawn by consent under the 1880 settlement. Rockefeller did not appear in Clarion; the coordinate marks the court that indicted him.
stops.campa: A grand jury in Clarion County returns an indictment against John D. Rockefeller and eight associates for conspiracy to secure a monopoly of the oil trade, to oppress producers, and to extort from the carriers. He does not appear. A requisition for him goes to the governor of New York, where he now lives, and sits in that office undecided from July onward. On the fifth of February 1880 the case ends by nolle prosequi, folded into a settlement among Standard, the producers, and the railroads. Whether the governor of New York would ever have signed the requisition is not on the record.
suggested_refs: The Clarion County indictment of 1879 and the compromise of February 1880, in Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, vol. 1, ch. 8
sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

stops.name: 140 Pearl Street, the Trust Agreement is signed
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the New York venue is taken from the chronology of the research pool and from the trust's own seat at 140 Pearl Street, against a geography entry in the same pool that placed the signing in downtown Cleveland. Nothing found puts the execution in Ohio. Sources also differ on whether there were 41 or 42 original certificate holders; the discrepancy is left standing.
stops.campa: In the offices at 140 Pearl Street the shareholders of some forty corporations sign their stock over to nine trustees and take back trust certificates. Seventy million dollars of capital, forty-two original holders by the Archive Center's count, one board. Samuel Dodd, who drafted it, has built a body no state charter describes and no state court has jurisdiction to reach, because it is not a corporation at all. Rockefeller is forty-two years old. Twenty-seven years later he set down in print what he thought the arrangement was.
stops.quote: The day of individual competition in large affairs is past and gone -- you might just as well argue that we should go back to hand labour and throw away our efficient machines -- and the sober good sense of the people will accept this fact when they have studied and tried it out.
stops.quote_source: John D. Rockefeller, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Chapter III, 'The Standard Oil Company'
suggested_refs: The Standard Oil Trust Agreement of 2 January 1882, drafted by Samuel C. T. Dodd
sources: Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Project Gutenberg #17090

stops.name: 4 West 54th Street, the brownstone off Fifth Avenue
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Rockefeller Archive Center); month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He buys a brownstone at 4 West 54th Street, a block off Fifth Avenue, as Standard Oil business draws him east more and more of the year, and the family's center of gravity follows the business. The house is large, heavy, and unfashionable, and its owner is uninterested in what the avenue makes of it. Cleveland stays the summer address at Forest Hill; New York becomes the working one, and remains so for the rest of his life. The children are raised here on chores, allowances, and a ledger apiece, in the household of the richest man in the country.
suggested_refs: 4 West 54th Street, Manhattan, the Rockefeller family house

stops.name: 26 Broadway, the address becomes the thing
stops.date_confidence: the headquarters move is attested to 1885, the building itself built 1884-85 (NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, LP-1930); month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Standard Oil takes the building at 26 Broadway, at the foot of the island, and within a few years the number is shorthand for the thing itself. From these rooms the trustees run refineries in a dozen states, pipelines, tank cars, barrel works, tin shops, and a selling apparatus that reaches every country store in America and a good part of Europe and Asia. Rockefeller keeps no visible court. He works at a plain desk, takes a plain lunch, and holds his conferences with committee heads who are asked for figures rather than opinions.
suggested_refs: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report, 'Standard Oil Building, 26 Broadway' (LP-1930)

stops.name: New York City, sworn before the Senate committee on trusts
stops.date_confidence: Tarbell (vol. 2, ch. 14) is explicit that the first investigation of importance sat in February 1888 in NEW YORK CITY at the direction of the New York State Senate. The research pool's Albany State Capitol coordinate, 220km away, is rejected on that authority. The exact hearing room was not identified and the coordinate is a general lower Manhattan point; the day defaults within the attested month.
stops.campa: A committee of the New York State Senate takes up the trusts, sits in the city in February, and calls him. He appears, answers what his counsel permits, and declines the rest with a courtesy that infuriates the room. The trust agreement itself is produced under compulsion, and the public sees for the first time the instrument that has governed the oil business for six years. He is forty-eight, and it is the first time he has had to explain himself under oath in front of anyone.
suggested_refs: Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, vol. 2, ch. 14, on the 1888 New York Senate investigation
sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

stops.name: Lima, the sour crude and the chemist
stops.date_confidence: the Lima commitment runs 1885-1889 and Frasch's process is attested to 1888 (PBS American Experience); the month is set to place the stop after the February hearing.
stops.campa: Northwest Ohio is producing crude nobody can sell. It stinks of sulphur, refines into a lamp oil that fouls wicks and blackens ceilings, and the trade calls it skunk oil. Against the flat opposition of his own committee he buys it anyway, field after field, at a few cents a barrel, until Standard is holding some forty million barrels in tankage while the objectors watch. He also hires a chemist named Herman Frasch and pays him to solve it. In 1888 Frasch takes the sulphur out.
suggested_refs: Herman Frasch's desulfurization process and the Lima-Indiana field

stops.name: Columbus, the Ohio court dissolves the Trust
stops.date_confidence: date corrected. State ex rel. Attorney General v. Standard Oil Co., 49 Ohio St. 137, was decided 2 March 1892; 21 March 1892, the date carried in the research pool, is the trustees' own dissolution resolution, and the pool had fused the two events onto the later date. The Columbus coordinate for the seat of the court is sound. Rockefeller was not present.
stops.campa: The attorney general of Ohio sues, and on the second of March the Ohio Supreme Court holds that Standard Oil of Ohio exceeded its corporate powers when it handed itself over to the trustees. On the twenty-first the trustees resolve to dissolve. The Trust ends as a legal form and does not end as a fact; the same men hold the same stocks and meet in the same rooms. Seven years later New Jersey, whose law permits a corporation to own the stock of other corporations, supplies the vessel, and Standard Oil of New Jersey becomes the holding company for all of it.
suggested_refs: State ex rel. Attorney General v. Standard Oil Co., 49 Ohio St. 137 (1892)
sources: Commercial and Financial Chronicle report of the trustees' resolution, cited via Rockefeller Archive Center

stops.name: Pocantico Hills, buying the ridge above the Hudson
stops.date_confidence: the assembly of the estate is attested from 1893 (Rockefeller Brothers Fund, Kykuit history); month and day default to 01. Kykuit itself is not built until 1905-1913 and its final form is credited substantially to John D. Rockefeller Jr.
stops.campa: He begins buying land above the Hudson at Pocantico Hills, parcel by parcel, until he holds thousands of acres of ridge and river an hour north of the city. He lays out the carriage roads himself and moves them when a view comes out wrong; he shifts full-grown trees on rollers to set them where he wants them. What he is buying here is ground and quiet, and the house comes long after: Kykuit will not stand until 1913, and its shape will owe as much to his son as to him.
suggested_refs: Kykuit and the Pocantico Hills estate, Sleepy Hollow, New York
sources: Rockefeller Brothers Fund, Kykuit history overview

stops.name: Forest Hill, the retirement nobody is told about
stops.date_confidence: the research pool's entry dates the withdrawal to 1896 while citing PBS, whose timeline actually says 1895; the range should read 1895-1897 and the earlier bound is not settled. Month and day default to 01. The coordinate is the Forest Hill estate, his Cleveland summer place; the withdrawal itself had no single location and was never announced.
stops.campa: In his middle fifties his health gives way: digestion, nerves, and an alopecia that takes every hair on his head and leaves him looking twenty years older within a season. He withdraws from the daily conduct of Standard Oil gradually and without announcement, in a manner designed to keep the press and the public from knowing, and lets John D. Archbold run the business. He remains president of Standard Oil of New Jersey on paper until 1911, and answers publicly for everything the company does in those sixteen years.
suggested_refs: Forest Hill, the Rockefeller summer estate at Cleveland Heights and East Cleveland

stops.name: Cobb Hall, one of two visits to the university he built
stops.date_confidence: the Rockefeller Archive Center records only two personal visits to the University of Chicago, in 1896 and 1901; month and day default to 01. The building he entered is not specified in the source, and Cobb Hall, the university's original main building, stands here as the campus landmark.
stops.campa: The University of Chicago has been open four years. He put six hundred thousand dollars into the first million in 1890, on condition that others match it, and by 1910 his gifts will run to some thirty-five million, closing with a check for ten million and a refusal to have anything named after him. He comes to see the place twice in his life, this year and again in 1901, and both times declines any part in running it. An interviewer asks him in 1901 what quality has counted for most.
stops.quote: I do not think there is any other quality so essential to success of any kind as the quality of perseverance. It overcomes almost everything, even nature.
stops.quote_source: Orison Swett Marden, How They Succeeded: Life Stories of Successful Men Told by Themselves (1901), ch. XII, 'John D. Rockefeller', p. 207; Project Gutenberg #64059
suggested_refs: Cobb Hall, the original main building of the University of Chicago
sources: Orison Swett Marden, How They Succeeded (1901), Project Gutenberg #64059

stops.name: 26 Broadway, the Mesabi ore sold to United States Steel
stops.date_confidence: the sale is attested to 1901 (PBS American Experience) and the month is set to place it during the formation of U.S. Steel. Figures conflict and are not reconciled: the research pool's $80 million covers the ore properties alone, mines plus lake fleet come to roughly $88.5 million, and several standard accounts give $90 million for the whole package. Nothing reached places Rockefeller personally on the Mesabi Range; the coordinate is his own headquarters.
stops.campa: He had gone into iron ore the way he went into oil, by accident first and then completely: mines on the Mesabi Range taken in on defaulted loans, a railroad down to the lakehead, a fleet of ore boats built to his order. J. P. Morgan is assembling United States Steel and cannot leave that ore outside it. Nothing in the record puts Rockefeller himself on the Mesabi Range. The mines go for eighty million dollars, the boats for eight and a half more, and some accounts put the whole package at ninety.
suggested_refs: The 1901 sale of the Mesabi ore properties and the Rockefeller lake fleet to United States Steel
sources: American Heritage, 'The Deal of the Century'

stops.name: 127 East 50th Street, the Institute opens in rented rooms
stops.date_confidence: incorporation attested to 13 June 1901. Coordinate corrected: the Institute began in temporary laboratories at 127 East 50th Street. The York Avenue campus given in the research pool for this date did not open until 11 May 1906 and belongs to that later year.
stops.campa: Frederick Taylor Gates, the Baptist minister who has been organizing the giving since 1891, reads a textbook of medicine on a summer holiday and comes back convinced that American medicine is largely guesswork and that endowed research, left alone, could end it. The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research is incorporated on the thirteenth of June and opens in rented laboratories on East 50th Street. Rockefeller's own grandson had died of scarlet fever the year before. The buildings on York Avenue, and the name Rockefeller University, come later.
suggested_refs: The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, later Rockefeller University

stops.name: Warwick Neck, the son marries a senator's daughter
stops.date_confidence: date attested. Place corrected: the marriage took place at Indian Oaks, the Aldrich summer house on Warwick Neck, Kent County, Rhode Island, not at Providence, which the research pool gave and which is where the couple first met in 1894. Whether John D. Rockefeller Sr. attended in person is not established by anything reached.
stops.campa: At Indian Oaks, the Aldrich family's summer house on Warwick Neck, John D. Rockefeller Junior marries Abby Greene Aldrich, daughter of Nelson W. Aldrich of Rhode Island, a power in the Republican Senate and in every question of tariff and currency that comes before it. The oil fortune and that political machinery are joined in one drawing room on a Rhode Island point. The couple had met seven years earlier at a friend's house in Providence, when neither family had any particular reason to notice the other.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Archive Center, 'Abby Aldrich Rockefeller'; Rhode Island Heritage Hall of Fame
sources: Rhode Island Heritage Hall of Fame

stops.name: 26 Broadway, the history in McClure's and the board for schools
stops.date_confidence: the first installment is attested to the November 1902 issue of McClure's (Poynter); the General Education Board is attested to 1902, incorporated 1903 (Rockefeller Archive Center). The series was Tarbell's own labor and is cited here as the event Standard read and did not answer; the coordinate is Standard's headquarters, not hers.
stops.campa: In the November number of McClure's, Ida Tarbell begins a history of the Standard Oil Company that will run through nineteen installments and be read by more Americans than have read anything else about him. She works from court records, from the repealed South Improvement charter, from the ledgers and the testimony of men he ruined. Standard's answer is silence: no suit and no statement from 26 Broadway. The same season he charters the General Education Board, to promote education in the United States without distinction of race, sex, or creed.
suggested_refs: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, serialized in McClure's Magazine, November 1902 to 1904
sources: Poynter, 'Today in Media History: Ida Tarbell's 1902-1904 investigative series'

stops.name: Chicago, Judge Landis names a number
stops.date_confidence: the fine is attested to 1907 and the Seventh Circuit reversal to 1908 (Standard Oil Co. of Indiana v. United States, 164 F. 376). The exact day is taken from the standard accounts of the judgment and is not independently confirmed here. Rockefeller was not in the courtroom; the coordinate marks the federal court that imposed the fine.
stops.campa: In a federal courtroom in Chicago, Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis fines Standard Oil of Indiana twenty-nine million two hundred and forty thousand dollars for taking rebates on the Chicago and Alton. It is the largest corporate penalty imposed in the country to that date, and it falls on one company of the old combination rather than on the combination itself. The Seventh Circuit reverses the judgment the following year, and the sum is never restored on retrial. Rockefeller is not in the room.
suggested_refs: Standard Oil Co. of Indiana v. United States, 164 F. 376 (7th Cir. 1908)
sources: Standard Oil Co. of Indiana v. United States, 164 F. 376 (7th Cir. 1908), as summarized in legal-historical accounts

stops.name: 4 West 54th Street, the World prints his father's other name
stops.date_confidence: date attested for the New York World investigation by A. B. Macdonald, as reproduced in later biographical treatments; the original newspaper page was not viewed. The investigation and its geography were the World's; this stop is placed at Rockefeller's own house because the revelation was about his family, and nothing reached records where he was or what he said.
stops.campa: A reporter for the New York World named A. B. Macdonald prints what the family has spent thirty years keeping down: that the itinerant cancer specialist calling himself Doctor William Levingston, long since dead, was William Avery Rockefeller, and that he had kept a second wife and a second household while the first was living. The richest man in America is revealed as the son of a bigamist and a mountebank. The papers run it for weeks. What he said about it, to anyone, is not in the record reached here.
suggested_refs: The New York World investigation of William Avery Rockefeller, February 1908
sources: New York World investigative report by A. B. Macdonald, as reproduced and summarized in later biographical treatments

stops.name: Pocantico Hills, the book that is not an autobiography
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1909 (Doubleday, Page & Co.); month and day default to 01. Where the book was dictated is not established by anything reached, and the coordinate is his own principal country residence in those years rather than an attested writing place.
stops.campa: He is seventy, and he publishes a book, put together from pieces dictated over several years, which takes care to say on its own first pages that it is neither a formal nor a complete autobiography. It is genial, anecdotal, and evasive by design. The rebates get a paragraph. The Cleveland purchases get a sentence. What it defends is not the conduct but the principle, that combination is the natural successor of competition in large affairs. On money itself he is less guarded than anywhere else in it.
stops.quote: I know of nothing more despicable and pathetic than a man who devotes all the waking hours of the day to making money for money's sake.
stops.quote_source: John D. Rockefeller, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Chapter I, 'Some Old Friends'
suggested_refs: Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (Doubleday, Page & Co., 1909), Project Gutenberg #17090
sources: Rockefeller Archive Center dossier summary of Random Reminiscences (1909)

stops.name: 26 Broadway, the hookworm million and the pedigree office
stops.date_confidence: the Rockefeller Sanitary Commission is attested to 1909 with an initial million dollars across eleven Southern states (Rockefeller Archive Center); month and day default to 01 and the stop is dated 1910 to carry both items. The Eugenics Record Office material is [R]: three atlas files carry a sentence funding it on 'Harriman, Rockefeller and Carnegie money' in 1910, and since the Rockefeller Foundation was not chartered until 1913, the 1910 money is inferred, not attested, to be Sr.'s personal giving. Rockefeller never travelled either to the hookworm districts or to Cold Spring Harbor; the coordinate is the office the money left from.
stops.campa: Gates finds him a disease. Hookworm has been draining the American South for generations, mistaken for laziness and for bad blood, and it costs about fifty cents a case to cure. The Rockefeller Sanitary Commission opens with a million dollars and works eleven states. In the same years Rockefeller money reaches the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, beside Andrew Carnegie's, to collect family pedigrees and build the case for sterilizing the unfit. Both enterprises are described, by the men running them, as the improvement of a people.
stops.quote: 'I am no beggar,' I have heard many of them say, to which I could only reply: 'I am sorry you feel that way about it.' I have been this sort of beggar all my life.
stops.quote_source: John D. Rockefeller, Random Reminiscences of Men and Events (1909), Chapter III
suggested_refs: The Rockefeller Sanitary Commission for the Eradication of Hookworm Disease; the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor
sources: alexander_graham_bell.journey.json, prescott_bush.journey.json, andrew_carnegie.journey.json (Eugenics Record Office funding sentence)

stops.name: The Capitol, the Supreme Court orders the combination broken
stops.date_confidence: decision attested to the day, Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1. Coordinate corrected: in 1911 the Court sat in the Old Senate Chamber of the U.S. Capitol, roughly 38.8899 / -77.0091; the research pool's 38.8898 / -77.0045 is the 1935 Supreme Court Building, which did not yet exist. Rockefeller was not present. The peak-fortune figure that follows is contested, commonly given as about $900 million circa 1912-1913.
stops.campa: In the Old Senate Chamber of the Capitol, the Court still sitting there a generation before it has a building of its own, Chief Justice White reads the opinion. The Sherman Act forbids unreasonable restraints of trade; Standard Oil is one; the combination is to be dissolved into its constituent companies within six months. Thirty-four companies come out of it, and Rockefeller holds a proportionate share of every one. In the two years afterward the separately quoted successor stocks carry his fortune to its recorded peak.
suggested_refs: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911)
sources: Justia U.S. Supreme Court Center, Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911)

stops.name: Albany, the Foundation chartered by the State of New York
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: New York Laws of 1913, Chapter 488, approved 14 May 1913. Rockefeller's personal presence at Albany is not claimed by the sources reached; the coordinate marks the legislature that granted the charter.
stops.campa: A federal charter had been sought first, and failed. Congress would not vote a perpetual body of that size into existence, and the objection was stated plainly on the floor: no private fortune should be permitted to organize itself into a permanent power. New York State grants it instead, on the fourteenth of May, to promote the well-being of mankind throughout the world. The endowment is about a hundred million dollars, and the charter sets no term and names no program.
suggested_refs: New York Laws of 1913, Chapter 488, the charter of the Rockefeller Foundation

stops.name: 26 Broadway, the tents burn in Colorado
stops.date_confidence: the Ludlow Massacre is attested to 20 April 1914 (Britannica). This stop is deliberately NOT placed at Ludlow: Rockefeller Sr. was not there, and the research pool's own caution is that Colorado Fuel & Iron policy and the answering Congressional testimony belong to John D. Rockefeller Jr., on whose file a Ludlow stop would properly sit. The coordinate is the New York office where the holding was owned and the news arrived.
stops.campa: The Rockefellers hold the controlling interest in Colorado Fuel and Iron, whose southern coal camps have been on strike since September and living in tents since the company evicted them from company housing. The policy is his son's, and so is the testimony that will answer for it before Congress; the name that attaches to the day is the family's. On the twentieth of April the Colorado National Guard and men in the company's pay fire into the Ludlow colony and burn it, and women and children die in a pit dug under a tent floor.
suggested_refs: The Ludlow tent colony site, Las Animas County, Colorado
sources: john_d_rockefeller_sr dossier lead on Colorado Fuel & Iron

stops.name: Pocantico Hills, Laura dies while he is in Florida
stops.date_confidence: death attested to 12 March 1915, of a heart attack, with Rockefeller in Florida (Rockefeller Archive Center, 'Laura Spelman Rockefeller'). The RAC page is ambiguous about where she died; Britannica and Find a Grave give Pocantico Hills, and the funeral was held there on 15 March. The research pool's claim that this fell 'roughly a year' after the fiftieth anniversary is wrong: that anniversary was 8 September 1914, six months earlier.
stops.campa: Laura dies of a heart attack on the twelfth of March, at seventy-six, and the funeral is held at Pocantico three days later. He is in Florida when it happens and does not reach her. They had been married fifty years and six months; the golden anniversary had been kept the previous September, with the whole family assembled. He does not marry again. In 1918 he sets up a fund in her name, the Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial, which will carry the social sciences in America for a decade before it is folded back into the Foundation.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Archive Center, 'Laura Spelman Rockefeller'

stops.name: Lakewood, the newspapers count to a billion
stops.date_confidence: the Lakewood winters are attested for roughly 1915-1918 and the billionaire reports to 1916 (Rockefeller Archive Center; PBS American Experience); month and day default to 01. The exact estate address within Lakewood was not confirmed and the coordinate marks the town. The billion-dollar valuation was disputed by his own advisers, and later historians commonly keep a peak of about $900 million.
stops.campa: He winters now at Lakewood among the New Jersey pines, in a place he calls Golf House, and the day is cut to the quarter hour: numbered golf balls, a bicycle ridden between shots, lunch at a fixed time, a nap taken flat on a bench with a paper over his face. In this year the newspapers report that his holdings have crossed a billion dollars and hand him the title he never loses, the first billionaire. His own people dispute the arithmetic. Historians since have generally put the peak lower.
suggested_refs: The Lakewood, New Jersey winter estate

stops.name: Forest Hill, the house burns down
stops.date_confidence: attested to the night of 17 December 1917 (Encyclopedia of Cleveland History and Cleveland Historical, 'Forest Hill'). The cause was never conclusively proven.
stops.campa: On the night of the seventeenth of December the Forest Hill house burns to the ground: some seven hundred acres of Cleveland summer estate, assembled from 1873 around a converted hotel that had failed, where his children learned to swim and where he had taken the cure of his own collapse in the nineties. He is seventy-eight, and he does not come back to Cleveland after it. Investigators find two empty five-gallon oil cans near the ruins and suspect two men who had worked on the place. Nothing is ever proved.
suggested_refs: Forest Hill Park, Cleveland Heights and East Cleveland, donated by John D. Rockefeller Jr. in 1938

stops.name: Ormond Beach, the house called The Casements
stops.date_confidence: the purchase is attested to 1918; the house was built in 1913 for the Rev. Dr. Harwood Huntington (City of Ormond Beach; Daytona Beach City tourism page). Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He buys a shingled house on the Halifax River at Ormond Beach, named for its casement windows and built five years earlier for a clergyman, and winters in it for the rest of his life. The days go: golf in the morning, a drive, church on Sunday, and dimes handed out to whoever is met along the way, caddies, waitresses, children, reporters. Henry Ford comes to see him here, and Harvey Firestone, and Thomas Edison. He is seventy-nine when he buys the place and will spend nineteen winters in it.
suggested_refs: The Casements, 25 Riverside Drive, Ormond Beach, Florida, now the city's cultural center
sources: Daytona Beach City tourism page, 'The Casements'

stops.name: Ormond Beach, death at The Casements
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Rockefeller Archive Center). Cause of death is [R]: sclerotic myocarditis is given by his grandson David Rockefeller in later recollection, other secondary accounts simplify it to arteriosclerosis, and no death certificate was located or examined.
stops.campa: He dies in his bed at The Casements in the early hours of the twenty-third of May, seven weeks short of his ninety-eighth birthday. He is asleep and does not wake. He has outlived the Trust by forty-five years and the dissolution decree by twenty-six. Laura has been dead twenty-two years. The cause of death, stated afterward by his grandson David, is sclerotic myocarditis; other accounts say arteriosclerosis, and no certificate has been produced.
suggested_refs: The Casements, Ormond Beach, Florida

stops.name: Lake View Cemetery, the obelisk that waited thirty-eight years
stops.date_confidence: burial attested to 27 May 1937, four days after the death. Coordinate reconciled: the research pool carried 41.5205 / -81.5920 in one lens, which falls about 900m north of the cemetery, and 41.5122 / -81.5892 in another; the cemetery itself sits at 41.5125 / -81.5919. The monument's height is disputed and left so: Cleveland Historical and the cemetery say 70 feet, Cleveland Magazine measures 65 feet 10 inches and 135 tons.
stops.campa: He is buried on the twenty-seventh in the family plot at Lake View, on a hilltop he had picked out himself as a trustee of the cemetery, beside Laura. The obelisk over him is Barre granite in four pieces, carved by Italian hands, shipped into Cleveland in 1899 and standing thirty-eight years before it had anything to mark. Getting one spire section past the railroad tracks took a special rig and eight months of assembly. It is the tallest stone on the ground. Visitors leave dimes at the foot of it.
suggested_refs: The Rockefeller monument, Lake View Cemetery, Cleveland
sources: Cleveland Historical, 'John D. Rockefeller Grave' and 'Rockefeller Monument in Lake View Cemetery'
